strengths: Addresses an important problem: user-level private federated learning for large ASR models. Speaker-partitioned datasets and LibriSpeech-to-Common Voice adaptation provide useful benchmarks with natural heterogeneity and domain shift.

The English clipping improvement is substantial. At σ_DP = 3×10^-6, Table 1 reports test WER decreasing from 31.1% with global clipping to 20.4% with dimension-based per-layer clipping under the same simulated conditions.

Extensive experiments examine initialization, cohort size, data heterogeneity, optimizers, augmentation, and three languages. The layer-specific noise experiments provide additional insight beyond aggregate accuracy comparisons.

Public datasets, detailed training configurations, compute reporting, and a code link support reproducibility. The manuscript explicitly identifies extrapolated results and the non-private seed-data assumption, and discusses deployment privacy requirements.
weaknesses: The claimed convergence rate is not established. Corollary 1 requires κ = 1−8(1−η_loc T_loc)^2 > 0, but its schedule η_loc = Θ(1/(L√(T_loc T))) makes κ approach −7 for fixed T_loc as T increases. Separately, Appendix F.5, Eqs. (33)–(34), uses independence between the LAMB preconditioner and DP noise, although Eqs. (11)–(15) compute that preconditioner from the noisy update. These are substantive gaps in a central theoretical contribution.

The headline privacy–utility trade-offs are extrapolations rather than jointly demonstrated results. The relevant English experiments use 34,753 users and cohorts of 1,024; Table 1 reports ε approximately 1.2×10^8 for the run associated with the extrapolated ε = 7.2 result. Useful guarantees require hypothetical populations of roughly 7–70 million and cohorts of 204,800, while assuming preserved WER. The disclosure is welcome, but non-private scaling to cohorts of 5,120 does not validate this assumption for noisy training.

The privacy accountant and implemented mechanism need reconciliation. Theorem 1 assumes independent Bernoulli sampling, whereas Algorithm 1, line 4, fixes cohort size. Furthermore, under Bernoulli sampling, the stated per-client noise produces aggregate variance conditional on the sampled cohort size; its exact equivalence to fixed-variance Gaussian noise in Appendix I.1 is not justified. A matching sampling and noise analysis is necessary for the formal guarantees.

The claimed benefit of combining LAMB with per-layer clipping is incompletely isolated. Tables 8–9 compare optimizers without DP, while the principal DP comparisons retain LAMB throughout. A matched optimizer-by-clipping ablation under DP would establish whether layer-wise adaptive normalization is essential to the improvement. This matters because both algorithmic ingredients are established prior methods.

Experiments use one 255M-parameter transformer architecture and do not report variability across independent training runs. Consequently, the small per-layer clipping improvements for French and German and the broader claims across large-model settings remain insufficiently supported. Despite the valuable empirical benchmark, the theoretical and privacy–utility support gaps prevent acceptance in the current form.
